A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InvAD research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original InvAD detection, localization, efficiency, and ablation results, including industrial benchmarks in Tables 2–7 and medical benchmarks in appendix Table 12.

after.justification: v3 retains original industrial and medical benchmark results and reports additional component-ablation and score-distribution analyses.

M1.justification: The feature-space diffusion model, few-step DDIM inversion, training objective, and anomaly scoring remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and Equations 1–8 retain the same procedure. The newly described feature extraction details and additional ablation configurations do not establish a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MVTecAD, VisA, MPDD, and the same six constituent medical datasets in BMAD. BMAD moves from v2's appendix into v3's main text. Changes to single-class evaluation and backbone studies concern experimental configurations within retained data and task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds MDM to Table 2's MVTecAD comparison and replaces DeCoDiff with DiAD in the transfer experiment in Table 5. The single-class MVTecAD comparison changes from DiffAD, GLAD, TransFusion, DAD, DDAD, ScoreDD, and DeCoDiff in v2 Table 3 to DiAD, TransFusion, OmiAD, DeCoDiff, and MDM in v3 Figure 1. The single-class VisA comparison and many qualitative comparators are removed.

E3.justification: The new component study introduces controls without inversion or feature-space modeling and compares single-step with multi-step inversion. The feature-encoder ablation replaces VAE and ResNet-18 with ViT-B. Transfer and backbone studies replace image-level evaluation across MVTecAD and VisA with image- and pixel-level evaluation on MVTecAD; standalone single-class VisA evaluation disappears. Default training budgets and the three-step inference configuration remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds the joint feature-space/inversion component ablation in Table 6 and hazelnut score histograms at 5 and 500 steps in Figure 4. Transfer and backbone analyses are revised, while extensive localization comparisons are removed. v3 Figure 3 retains three cases from v2's appendix montage. The scoring ablation in v3 Table 9 already appeared in v2 Table 13.

E5.justification: Both versions state that random seeds were fixed and nondeterministic GPU operations disabled where possible. Neither reports repeated-run counts, numerical seed values, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across runs.

E6.justification: Substantial category-level and qualitative results are removed, while component, DiAD-transfer, MDM-baseline, and histogram results are added. Retained Table 2 results are unchanged. In the BMAD InvAD row, OCT2017 AU-ROC changes from 99.2 to 99.0, mAD from 87.4 to 87.2, and FPS from 64.3 to 88. The MVTecAD DiT-base ablation changes from 94.4 to 93.8 image AU-ROC. These are reported result changes; the PDFs do not establish why they changed.

T1.justification: Equations 1–21, including the diffusion formulations and appendix derivation of DDIM inversion, retain the same mathematical content. The new reverse-scoring discussion provides empirical interpretation without adding or revising a formal result.

C1.justification: The central claims remain reconstruction-free anomaly detection through few-step latent inversion, perturbation-timestep tuning avoidance, plug-and-play applicability, and competitive accuracy with faster inference. The abstract's change from three datasets to four industrial and medical benchmarks reflects BMAD evidence and applicability claims already present in v2.

C2.justification: New Section 9 connects degradation with additional inversion steps to reverse scoring in high-dimensional distributions. The component discussion interprets the contributions of feature-space modeling and inversion. Transfer discussion changes from acknowledging DeCoDiff accuracy losses to describing gains for DiAD and MDM. The limitation of requiring more than one function evaluation remains.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies EfficientNet block selection, feature interpolation and concatenation, feature dimensions, and ViT/DINO token extraction. It also supplies training-time and GPU-memory information. These are additional disclosures about implementation and resources. v2's small-test-set throughput batch-size caveat and project-page link disappear, while the code link and principal hyperparameter and hardware specifications remain.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including MAD-AD, On Diffusion Modeling for Anomaly Detection, ViT, ADPretrain, and PyTorch, and supplies references for previously compared methods such as SimpleNet and PaDiM. ResNet and latent-diffusion references disappear with their encoder ablations. The related-work taxonomy and central novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The title adds InvAD, an author affiliation changes, and headings and citations adopt numbered formatting. BMAD and scoring-ablation discussions move into the main experiments, and the supplement is reorganized. Most background, methodology, and conclusion prose is retained.

P2.justification: v3 introduces a front-page accuracy–speed plot, a component-ablation table, and score histograms. It replaces the detailed single-class MVTecAD table with a plot, removes the single-class VisA table and full-page localization montages, and retains selected cases in a compact panel. Multiple tables change structure and styling, while BMAD and scoring tables move into the main text.

improvement.justification: The new component ablation, reverse-scoring analysis, and feature-extraction details improve method validation and reproducibility. However, removing detailed single-class comparisons and most localization examples reduces comparative evidence. v3 also leaves an unexplained MDM discrepancy: 87.2 image AU-ROC in Table 2 versus 91.9 in Table 5, both described as multi-class MVTecAD comparisons. These benefits, losses, and unresolved consistency issues prevent a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
